\chapter{Hacer, Decir, and the -go Verb Club}
\label{ch:yo-go-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{70}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use the three learned singular forms of hacer and decir and compare tengo, hago, and digo without predicting unseen verbs.}

Complete ES-C12-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate the chapter promise with known words and only the learned singular person frame.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[hacer]{hacer — doing or making with three singular forms}

\label{lesson:ES-C12-hacer}



\begin{quote}
You already use \textbf{tengo, tienes, tiene}, and you already know \textbf{café} and the question word \textbf{qué}. Reuse that small frontier for one verb that covers both English “do” and “make.”
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
The \textbf{h} in \textbf{hacer} is silent, just as it is in \textbf{hola}. In \textbf{hago}, the written \textbf{g} has the hard sound heard before \textbf{a}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{hacer} means “to do” or “to make.” It descends from Latin \textbf{facere}, with the same making root preserved in English \textbf{fact}, \textbf{factory}, and \textbf{manufacture}. Much of early Castilian changed word-initial Latin \textbf{f} into an \textbf{h} sound that later became silent, leaving the spelling as a historical trace.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: only the three singular forms}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present of \textbf{hacer}} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{hago} \\
tú & \textbf{haces} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{hace} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say the bounded set as \textbf{hago · haces · hace}. Only the learned \textbf{yo} form contains \textbf{g}. Compare it with the familiar \textbf{tengo}, but do not extend the comparison beyond forms you already own.

Use the forms with one known object:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Hago café.} — “I make coffee.”
  \item \textbf{Haces café.} — “You make coffee.”
  \item \textbf{Hace café.} — “He, she, or formal you makes coffee.”
\end{itemize}

You can also ask \textbf{¿Qué haces?} — “What are you doing?” Plural persons and weather expressions wait for later lessons.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “hacer — hago, haces, hace”
  \item “¿Qué haces? Hago café.”
  \item “facere — fact — factory — hacer”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What two English verbs does \emph{hacer} cover? (“Do” and “make.”) Give the three learned forms. (\emph{Hago, haces, hace.}) Which Latin source and English cousin help explain it? (\emph{Facere}; \emph{fact} or \emph{factory}.) Next: add \textbf{decir} without widening the person frame.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[decir]{decir — saying with the same small person frame}

\label{lesson:ES-C12-decir}



\begin{quote}
You can ask \textbf{cómo}, say \textbf{hola}, and retrieve \textbf{hago, haces, hace}. Keep those three persons fixed while adding the verb “to say.”
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
In \textbf{digo}, the \textbf{g} before \textbf{o} is hard. Keep the \textbf{i} in all three learned forms short and clear: \textbf{digo, dices, dice}.
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{decir} means “to say” or “to tell.” It descends from Latin \textbf{dīcere}, “to say.” English keeps the same root in \textbf{diction}, \textbf{dictionary}, \textbf{predict} (“say beforehand”), and \textbf{verdict} (“a true saying”).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one more three-form set}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present of \textbf{decir}} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{digo} \\
tú & \textbf{dices} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{dice} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{digo · dices · dice}. The \textbf{yo} form has \textbf{g}, while the other two learned forms do not. Do not build a full table or a general vowel-change rule from this small set yet.

Now combine it only with known language:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Digo hola.} — “I say hello.”
  \item \textbf{Dices hola.} — “You say hello.”
  \item \textbf{Dice hola.} — “He, she, or formal you says hello.”
  \item \textbf{¿Cómo dices “hola”?} — “How do you say ‘hello’?”
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “decir — digo, dices, dice”
  \item “Digo hola. ¿Cómo dices hola?”
  \item “dīcere — diction — decir”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{decir} mean? (“To say” or “to tell.”) Give the three learned forms. (\emph{Digo, dices, dice.}) Which Latin source and English cousin help explain it? (\emph{Dīcere}; \emph{diction}, \emph{dictionary}, or \emph{predict}.) Next: compare only the three \textbf{yo} forms you have actually learned.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tengo · hago · digo]{tengo · hago · digo — compare only what you know}

\label{lesson:ES-C12-yo-go}



\begin{quote}
Three learned verbs now place \textbf{g} in the \textbf{yo} form: \textbf{tengo, hago, digo}. Compare those three without guessing the form of any unseen verb.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one visible corner}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{infinitive} & \textbf{meaning} & \textbf{learned \textbf{yo} form} & \textbf{learned \textbf{tú} form} \\
\midrule
\textbf{tener} & to have & \textbf{tengo} & \textbf{tienes} \\
\textbf{hacer} & to do / make & \textbf{hago} & \textbf{haces} \\
\textbf{decir} & to say / tell & \textbf{digo} & \textbf{dices} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The shared observation is narrow: each learned \textbf{yo} form ends in \textbf{-go}, while each learned \textbf{tú} form does not. This is a memory organizer for three known forms, not permission to manufacture new ones.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
The three modern forms did not arise by attaching one productive Latin \textbf{-go} ending. Older stem sounds changed in different ways, and analogy helped common verbs converge on a familiar shape. That mixed history explains why the group is useful to remember but unsafe as a prediction rule.

Later lessons can introduce other verbs on their own evidence. For now, the complete comparison is exactly \textbf{tengo · hago · digo}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “tengo — hago — digo”
  \item “tienes — haces — dices”
  \item “a memory organizer, not a prediction machine”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which three learned \textbf{yo} forms end in \textbf{-go}? (\emph{Tengo, hago, digo.}) May this comparison predict an unseen verb? (No.) Why not? (Different sound histories and analogy converged on the same shape.) Next: retrieve the whole chapter without adding any word or form.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — doing, making, and saying in the singular}

\label{lesson:ES-C12-practice}



\begin{quote}
This checkpoint adds nothing. Retrieve two bounded three-form sets, use them with known words, and compare only \textbf{tengo, hago, digo}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the complete small chapter frame}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item doing or making: \textbf{hago · haces · hace}.
  \item saying or telling: \textbf{digo · dices · dice}.
  \item the learned \textbf{yo} comparison: \textbf{tengo · hago · digo}.
  \item known-word use: \textbf{Hago café. Digo hola. ¿Cómo dices “hola”?}
\end{itemize}

Plural persons, weather nouns, homework vocabulary, and unseen verbs remain outside this checkpoint.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{hacer} continues Latin \emph{facere}, the making family of \textbf{fact} and \textbf{factory}.
  \item \textbf{decir} continues Latin \emph{dīcere}, the saying family of \textbf{diction} and \textbf{predict}.
  \item inherited sound changes and analogy made three known \textbf{yo} forms converge on \textbf{-go}; the resemblance does not predict forms you have not learned.
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “hago, haces, hace”
  \item “digo, dices, dice”
  \item “tengo, hago, digo”
  \item “Hago café. Digo hola.”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give both three-form sets. (\emph{Hago, haces, hace; digo, dices, dice.}) Which three learned \textbf{yo} forms share \textbf{-go}? (\emph{Tengo, hago, digo.}) Why is that comparison a memory aid rather than a prediction rule? (Its mixed history does not license unseen forms.) The next chapter may now introduce its own verbs one at a time.
\end{tcolorbox}
